title: Intellectual Property Licensing — Practitioner Testimony Operator Workbook
subtitle: Choosing the licensing model, protecting the invention, running royalty math, finding licensees, negotiating the term sheet and commercializing research through technology transfer.

worksheets.title: Licensing Model and Protection Stack Builder
worksheets.purpose: Choose between manufacturing, assignment and licensing with evidence instead of excitement, then build a lean protection stack of research, assignment checks and a provisional filing so every pitch rests on perceived ownership and a fixed walk-away position.
instructions: Complete the business-model fields before touching search tools, because the path you choose shapes every protection decision that follows.
Back every royalty figure with a named practitioner range and state whether it applies to wholesale or gross sales.
Run the patent search by concept, group synonyms in parentheses, and loosen abstract filters before declaring the field empty.
Pull the assignment record yourself rather than trusting the assignee printed on the face of any patent.
Leave price for last in negotiation, but fix your private floor, minimums and indemnity position before the first meeting.

fields.name: business_model_fork
fields.prompt: Decide which of the three paths you will take: manufacture the product yourself, sell the rights outright through an assignment, or license them while keeping title. Write down the reasons that rule out the two paths you are rejecting today.
fields.example: Licensing, not venturing. Making the product would mean floating at least $250,000 in inventory while retailers pay in 60 to 90 days [inventRightTV — E5dH32uMqOY @ 00:05:05]. Assignment is out because buyers often offer far less than inventors expect, sometimes five thousand dollars against a million-dollar ask [Eric Hanscom (ICIP) — yUPS-UISPnQ @ 00:05:39]. Licensing keeps title and borrows a partner's shelf space.

fields.name: manufacturing_gate_check
fields.prompt: Test the manufacturing option against four conditions: strong demand, healthy margins, a clear sales channel, and the ability to manage operations. Note which conditions you can prove with evidence today and which ones are only hopes driven by excitement.
fields.example: Demand: unproven beyond friends. Margins: unknown until factory quotes arrive. Channel: no retail buyer relationships. Operations: no staff or warehouse. All four fail, so no manufacturing, echoing the warning not to manufacture just because someone called it a million-dollar idea [Patent Question — E7nUaZBoVeI @ 00:05:11]. The four-part gate itself comes from the same practitioner [Patent Question — E7nUaZBoVeI @ 00:05:27].

fields.name: target_royalty_band
fields.prompt: Record the royalty band you will treat as realistic for your category, citing at least two practitioner ranges. State whether the rate applies to wholesale or gross sales, and note how much sales volume the rate needs to matter.
fields.example: Working band of 3 to 5% of wholesale, inside the 2 to 10% of wholesale range that varies by industry [Patent Question — dlTT-hWgkB8 @ 00:00:43]. The broader 5 to 20% band carries a warning that real profit needs significant sales volume [UpCounsel — wiI7fBL42Vg @ 00:02:12]. Volume target: enough units that even 3% pays meaningfully.

fields.name: exclusivity_structure
fields.prompt: Choose the grant structure you will offer first: exclusive, co-exclusive, sole, or non-exclusive, plus any field-of-use or territory split. Explain how much market power you hold and why that power supports the structure you picked for this product.
fields.example: Exclusive grant only if the partner is picked very carefully; with market power, non-exclusive is the demand [Patent pc — A7xn_DzjKzE @ 00:01:04]. Plan: split by field of use, licensing a medical device into human and pet markets at the same time so a competitor with similar technology cannot arrive first [Licensing Consulting Group — 0MpPL7OXNr4 @ 00:01:34].

fields.name: fee_structure_mix
fields.prompt: Specify the payment mix you will propose: a fixed licensing fee, a running royalty, guaranteed annual minimums, per-unit caps, equity, or a combination. Explain why each element appears and which one the licensee will most likely resist.
fields.example: Fixed licensing fee at signing plus a running royalty, since some businesses pay both [Simple Explain — 2-_h0sI3YQI @ 00:02:31]. Annual minimums are non-negotiable so the licensee is pushed to sell as many covered products as possible [Michigan Engineering — EPj0ydCGdiU @ 00:03:03]. Expected resistance: the minimums. Price discussion is held until last because every other term moves it.

fields.name: next_best_alternative_value
fields.prompt: Estimate what your technology is worth by naming the licensee's next best alternative and what that alternative would cost them. Compare that figure against the quarter-to-a-third-of-profits rule of thumb and note where the two disagree before any meeting.
fields.example: Next best alternative: the licensee redesigning around the idea in-house, costing them engineering time and a delayed launch. That cost caps the value, because technology is worth no more than the licensee's next best alternative, and the quarter-to-a-third-of-profits rule is only a starting point [Kauffman FoundersSchool — q5uDRlH_eFo @ 00:01:41]. Gap noted: the rule overstates value.

fields.name: prior_art_search_log
fields.prompt: Log your concept-based Boolean search of the patent database. List the concepts and synonyms you grouped with parentheses, the hit counts before and after grouping, and whether you loosened any abstract filter before concluding nothing similar exists.
fields.example: Searched for the concept, not the word [Edel Patents — SDXhhmDKGJo @ 00:00:56]. Grouping synonyms inside parentheses cut one example query from 316 hits to 46. The abstract-only filter returned almost nothing, so it was loosened, since abstract searches narrow fast enough to drop important documents [Edel Patents — SDXhhmDKGJo @ 00:04:28]. Full-text coverage runs from 1976 onward.

fields.name: application_and_assignment_record
fields.prompt: Record the exact application number from the top left of the filing receipt, then pull the assignment record. List the current owner, any security interests, reel/frame bulk deals, name changes, and any unrecorded licenses you still need to rule out.
fields.example: Number copied from the receipt's top left before searching [Edel Patents — oOln2IDvhqE @ 00:01:47]. The assignee on the patent face was only current at issue, so the assignment record was pulled [USPTOvideo — np8RKbVMSLg @ 00:10:51]. One bank entry looked like a sale but was a security agreement, meaning loan collateral [Patents Demystified — zel57Kej5nY @ 00:06:15].

fields.name: provisional_filing_plan
fields.prompt: Plan your provisional filing for perceived ownership. Note your entity status and fee, confirm the draft discloses every implementation detail, set the same-day fee payment, and decide whether the licensee will be asked to fund the non-provisional application later.
fields.example: Micro entity, income under $150k, so the provisional costs $65 and buys perceived ownership [inventRightTV — CS31715RNQk @ 00:05:30]. Draft checked for every implementation detail and the fee paid the same day [Idea2PatentAI — ixENhsfAdEA @ 00:05:22]. Royalty offered on a 7/5/1 tier: seven if granted, five if pending, one if it never issues [inventRightTV — CS31715RNQk @ 00:11:10].

fields.name: pre_meeting_lockdown
fields.prompt: Before the first licensing meeting, write down your price, your annual minimums, your refusal to indemnify the manufacturer, and your refusal to permanently transfer title. Confirm a proprietary, protectable element is locked in before any pitch conversation begins.
fields.example: Price, annual minimums and no indemnity for the manufacturer, all fixed before the first meeting [John Ferrell, Esq. — Te8GX-Xx4mo @ 00:01:28]. Rights may be licensed, even exclusively, but never permanently transferred inside the license [John Ferrell, Esq. — Te8GX-Xx4mo @ 00:02:24]. Provisional on file, so the protection gate that stops deal conversations is cleared [The Sourcing Gals — 7aTTgSE0elA @ 00:24:41].

worksheets.completion_gate: Do not move to Worksheet 2 until a business path is chosen with the manufacturing gate documented, a provisional is filed or scheduled with the fee paid the same day, the assignment record is checked, and your price, minimums and no-indemnity position are written down.

worksheets.title: Royalty Math and Licensee Outreach Tracker
worksheets.purpose: Turn royalty rates into dollar projections grounded in store counts, lock minimum guarantees and reversion rights, and run a disciplined outreach campaign to 20 to 30 vetted companies with a two-sentence pitch, a working prototype and persistent follow-up.
instructions: Chart the volume math at 3%, 4%, 5% and 6% before naming any rate to a company.
Treat about 5% as the anchor and justify every point above it with completed CAD, testing or tooling.
Vet each target for complaints, lawsuits, outside-submission processes and NDA fairness before the first connection request.
Log every touch with its date so follow-ups land every five days until six or seven touches are reached.
Keep the day job funded through the one-to-two-year gap between signature and meaningful royalty checks.

fields.name: volume_math
fields.prompt: Run the volume math before any negotiation. Multiply the licensee's store count by roughly one sale a week per store, then chart annual royalty income at 3%, 4%, 5% and 6%. Decide whether the volume justifies an exclusive.
fields.example: A licensee with 2,000 stores at one sale a week per store moves about 104,000 units a year. Charted at 3%, 4%, 5% and 6% of wholesale, the spread decides the deal; if the volume is not there, walk or give only a non-exclusive [inventRightTV — 5pNsi_2H-J4 @ 00:02:17]. Here the volume supports an exclusive.

fields.name: royalty_rate_anchor
fields.prompt: Set your royalty anchor using the most common rate practitioners report, then adjust it up or down. List the work you have already done, such as CAD, testing or tooling, and whether the product is a high-volume consumable.
fields.example: Anchor at about 5%, the most common average seen across years of student deals [inventRightTV — 5pNsi_2H-J4 @ 00:04:38]. CAD files and testing are complete, which supports asking for seven or eight. Not a high-volume consumable, so no drop toward three. Cross-check: 3 to 6% of gross sales is the typical patent range [UpCounsel — mtxmo_OkhSw @ 00:00:30].

fields.name: percentage_timing
fields.prompt: Describe when and how you will name a percentage. Note whether you will let the company gather manufacturer quotes and calculate its own profit first, or walk in with written walk-away terms, and what evidence will move the needle upward.
fields.example: No percentage in the opening call; the first question is simply whether they are interested [The Patent Professor — bO09tLv7ysM @ 00:00:38]. Once they have factory quotes, their own profit figure becomes leverage for a convincing argument that a bigger royalty is affordable [inventRightTV — G2JXLQrTZXI @ 00:29:45]. Walk-away floor written privately beforehand: 4% with minimums.

fields.name: minimum_guarantees_and_reversion
fields.prompt: Write the minimum guarantee and required sales figures you will demand, plus the trigger that returns the rights to you. Include termination language for a licensee that sits on the product instead of manufacturing it after signing.
fields.example: Minimum guarantees are locked so the rights come back if the licensee does not perform [inventRightTV — 5pNsi_2H-J4 @ 00:03:37]. A rotating label carried guarantees from $250,000 to $750,000 per year across roughly 20 years [inventRightTV — Se-TzTVqhfY @ 00:02:18]. Termination applies if the licensee shelves the product [J.D. Houvener / Bold Patents Law Firm — 2yLgmvphmBw @ 00:05:03].

fields.name: improvements_and_enforcement
fields.prompt: Decide who owns improvements and version two, and who carries the cost of enforcing the patent. Note whether you would accept slightly lower royalties in exchange for placing enforcement on an exclusive licensee, and the reasoning behind that trade.
fields.example: Ownership of future versions stays with the inventor, so a manufacturer that improves the product during tooling cannot claim version two [J.D. Houvener / Bold Patents Law Firm — 2yLgmvphmBw @ 00:05:03]. Under the exclusive grant, a slightly lower royalty is traded for making the licensee carry the expensive job of enforcement [Jeff Schell — cfPpWt8cw64 @ 00:02:52]. Accepted trade: one point.

fields.name: cash_runway
fields.prompt: Estimate your personal cash runway from signature to meaningful royalties. Note how payments arrive, whether quarterly and on wholesale price, and how your day job or other income will fund the gap while sales build over time.
fields.example: Royalties figured as a percentage of the wholesale price and paid quarterly [Brian Fried - The Inventor Coach — UnGdjQb467o @ 00:01:58]. Budget one to two years from signature before checks really add up, with the day job covering the gap [inventRightTV — Se-TzTVqhfY @ 00:06:40]. Upside reference: one inventor's quarterly checks reached about $250,000 [inventRightTV — gxeuCPaGeHY @ 00:06:14].

fields.name: licensee_target_list
fields.prompt: Build a fit-checked list of 20 to 30 potential licensees. For each, note its product lines and retailers, whether it accepts outside submissions, any complaints or lawsuits found by search, and how one-sided its NDA appears.
fields.example: Twenty-six companies listed, because one deal may take reaching 20 to 30 and most inventors never bother [inventRightTV — IMLF0c7wOQI @ 00:00:51]. Each name searched with complaints and lawsuits; three were dropped for having no outside-submission process or a heavily one-sided NDA [inventRightTV — MvycxV2ib_8 @ 00:01:17]. Priority goes to partners already holding multiple retail SKUs.

fields.name: outreach_cadence
fields.prompt: Map your outreach cadence across LinkedIn, email and phone. Record connections per company, companies covered per session, the spacing between follow-ups, and the touch count you will reach before treating any company as unresponsive or closed.
fields.example: About ten LinkedIn connections per company with no note attached, five companies per 30-minute session [inventRightTV — 1w_iTE7ZNso @ 00:20:54]. Follow-ups every five days, since success tends to arrive at six to seven touches while 48 percent never follow up [inventRightTV — 1w_iTE7ZNso @ 00:27:54]. Going dark triggers a concern-first message asking whether everything is okay.

fields.name: two_sentence_pitch
fields.prompt: Draft your two-sentence pitch stating your IP status, what the product is, and its single most important benefit. Then list the cost and comparable price points you will have ready, since price is the leading reason products get rejected.
fields.example: Pitch covers IP status, product and benefit in two sentences [inventRightTV — 1w_iTE7ZNso @ 00:26:10]: provisional patent filed; a one-handed kitchen tool that cuts prep time. Manufacturing cost and three comparable shelf prices are on hand, because price is the number one reason products get kicked out [inventRightTV — 1w_iTE7ZNso @ 00:50:47].

fields.name: prototype_and_nda_readiness
fields.prompt: Confirm your demonstration readiness and confidentiality approach. Note the works-like prototype you can show, the backup demo recording, when you will ask for an NDA, and how you will handle a company asking to see IP.
fields.example: A cheap frankenstein works-like prototype is within reach, plus a backup demo recording because prototypes break [inventRightTV — biVTpLl2T5U @ 00:09:53]. Companies need to see the product does what is claimed [inventRightTV — p3ODWhpvt3E @ 00:02:07]. An NDA is requested only when they ask for IP or a prototype, an easy ask [inventRightTV — 1w_iTE7ZNso @ 00:48:53].

worksheets.completion_gate: Do not move to Worksheet 3 until the volume chart is complete, minimum guarantees and termination triggers are drafted, at least 20 vetted companies are listed, your two-sentence pitch is final, and a works-like prototype plus a backup demo recording are ready.

worksheets.title: Term Sheet, Grant Matrix and Technology Transfer Planner
worksheets.purpose: Lock the commercial skeleton in a short term sheet, then define scope, money, milestones and exit triggers for the definitive license, and apply the same discipline to university and research licensing where filings, inventorship and equity decide the outcome.
instructions: Mark each term-sheet clause as binding or non-binding; exclusivity and confidentiality are the usual binding pair.
Never hand over a right in the grant matrix that has no value attached to it.
Index any per-unit or foreign-currency royalty and write automatic reversion triggers before the deal closes.
For research inventions, file the provisional before any talk, poster or manuscript, including oral presentations.
Price equity as deferred compensation against high failure odds rather than as a substitute for diligence milestones.

fields.name: term_sheet_binding_clauses
fields.prompt: List the commercial skeleton of your short term sheet and mark which clauses will be binding. Separate non-binding business terms from binding exclusivity or no-shop, confidentiality, expenses and validity dates, and explain each choice in one line.
fields.example: Non-binding: royalty, territory, field and term. Binding: no-shop exclusivity and confidentiality, plus a validity date. The sheet exists to show how risk is shared, because many inventors lose out by not understanding deal mechanics [Trenner Law Firm - Patents & Trademarks — dSzZD5CnwK8 @ 00:03:52]. Payment uses a percentage of sales or a fixed fee per unit [UpCounsel — QaABLYw6maY @ 00:00:34].

fields.name: grant_of_rights_matrix
fields.prompt: Fill in the grant-of-rights matrix: exclusive, sole or non-exclusive; field of use; territory; and whether manufacture, use and sell rights are included. Flag any right you are handing over without a value attached to it before the definitive license is drafted.
fields.example: Exclusive in North American consumer retail, non-exclusive elsewhere, with manufacture and sell rights granted but no sublicensing. The grant language states the type outright, because discovering later that a license was non-exclusive leaves no way to stop a competitor [Ayers Law TV ~ Andrew M. Ayers, Esq. — lVFYoVaNnrs @ 00:04:35]. Pending-patent rights become active upon grant [UpCounsel — AaEw4SGbkk0 @ 00:02:27].

fields.name: royalty_and_hybrid_payment
fields.prompt: Set the royalty rate and payment architecture for the definitive license. Note your anchor rate, any upfront fee, rate-adjustment provisions tied to sales performance or industry shifts, and how distribution reach compares in importance to the headline rate.
fields.example: Anchor at about 5% inside a 3 to 7% band [Licensing Basics — uBnJLlSWMLk @ 00:02:31], accepting less from a licensee with far wider distribution, since distribution matters more than the specific rate [Licensing Basics — uBnJLlSWMLk @ 00:01:40]. Hybrid structure: upfront fee plus ongoing royalty, with rate adjustment tied to sales performance [UpCounsel — cURFfKlt_Ek @ 00:01:35].

fields.name: currency_and_indexation
fields.prompt: Identify every royalty that is fixed per unit or paid in a foreign currency, and write the indexation provision that protects it. Note the currency, the index you will reference, and how often the adjustment will be recalculated over the term.
fields.example: A fixed per-unit royalty paid in a foreign currency, which can deliver an exchange gain or lose badly, so proper indexation is written in [BaxterIPAttorneys — yl8L7tuwNuI @ 00:04:55]. The rule is simple: index every per-unit or foreign-currency royalty before signing [BaxterIPAttorneys — yl8L7tuwNuI @ 00:05:12]. Recalculation set annually against the agreed index.

fields.name: performance_and_milestones
fields.prompt: Write the performance obligations attached to an exclusive grant. Name each milestone, its deadline, and whether missing it gives you an explicit right to terminate or merely triggers good-faith renegotiation, and decide which outcome you will accept.
fields.example: Milestones: first production run within twelve months, retail launch within eighteen. Missing either gives an explicit right to terminate, distinct from good-faith renegotiation [Bao Tran, Esq. | Patent Attorney — SkIAUEkenak @ 00:13:01]. A performance clause lets the licensor exit if the product is shelved [J.D. Houvener / Bold Patents Law Firm — -VhDIVEwvzI @ 00:00:58].

fields.name: reversion_triggers
fields.prompt: List the automatic reversion triggers that return rights to you without negotiation. Cover bankruptcy, the licensee ceasing to operate, out-of-print or discontinued status, and decide whether a sale of the licensee company should also trigger reversion.
fields.example: Rights revert automatically on bankruptcy, on the licensee ceasing to operate, and on out-of-print status, all written before the deal closes [Boardgame Publisher — SOV77fL52Dw @ 00:04:37]. Sale of the licensee company is treated as a trigger too, since practitioners split on that point. Term length benchmark: one board game publisher asks for five-year terms.

fields.name: know_how_definition
fields.prompt: Document the know-how that travels with the license so it can be defined in the grant. List each item in summary bullet form, and note which items depend on a pending patent whose rights activate only upon grant.
fields.example: Know-how listed in summary bullets: assembly sequence, tooling tolerances, supplier specifications and test protocol, so it can actually be defined in the grant [BaxterIPAttorneys — yl8L7tuwNuI @ 00:02:40]. The pending-patent clause makes those rights active upon grant, with filing completed before any details were disclosed [UpCounsel — AaEw4SGbkk0 @ 00:02:27]. Each bullet is cross-referenced to the grant schedule.

fields.name: equity_vs_cash
fields.prompt: If the licensee is a cash-poor startup, decide whether to take equity in place of upfront cash. Record the stake range you will accept, the failure odds you are pricing in, and any liquidity-fee offset you will request.
fields.example: Equity of 2 to 5% in place of upfront cash, priced against a 90% chance it ends up worth nothing [Bao Tran, Esq. | Patent Attorney — SkIAUEkenak @ 00:09:28]. The university's liquidity fee is to be offset by its equity payout, and on sublicenses the spread over the university royalty stays with the startup [Osage University Partners — Q3YzwCiT2M4 @ 00:48:14].

fields.name: publication_and_inventorship_gate
fields.prompt: Before any talk, poster or manuscript goes public, confirm a provisional is on file. Record who selected the key compounds or designs, the agreed inventor contribution percentages, and every NDA, MOU and MTA signed with collaborating institutions.
fields.example: Provisional filed before the conference talk, because outside the US the invention is unpatentable the day it is published and oral presentations count [Salk Institute — 3iEjObMZnZo @ 00:49:36]. Compound selection was run in-house, since whoever picks the compounds is the inventor [Salk Institute — 3iEjObMZnZo @ 00:40:21]. Contribution splits and an MTA were signed before cross-institution work [USPTOvideo — hwcNfSr-ia0 @ 00:46:04].

fields.name: tech_transfer_economics
fields.prompt: Model the realistic income from a university-licensed invention. Note the provisional and non-provisional costs, the admin fee and inventor share in the revenue waterfall, the royalty base definition, and the lottery-like odds that any single invention pays off.
fields.example: Waterfall: a 15% admin fee and patent-cost recovery come off first, then inventors receive one third [Technology Licensing Office (TLO) — 2ADE7tP4bYM @ 00:10:33]. Odds: 0.1% of disclosed inventions ever reach $1M cumulative [OSU Center for Clinical and Translational Science — HKAvhkDKxNQ @ 00:27:16]. Royalty base defined to capture trademark and brand extensions [USPTOvideo — AcpNKjCol4s @ 00:33:37].

worksheets.completion_gate: This worksheet is complete when the term sheet marks binding clauses, the grant matrix states exclusivity type, field, territory and rights, every royalty is indexed where needed, termination and reversion triggers are written, and any research invention has a provisional on file before public disclosure.

worksheets.title: Brand Licensing Program and Portfolio Monetization Planner
worksheets.purpose: Turn a brand or patent portfolio into licensing income by fixing the royalty position, the minimum guarantee math, the scope of licensed products and the monetization route before any licensor, licensee, broker or funder conversation begins.
instructions: Gather your licensee's own year-one sales projection, your product cost, and the retail price of any unbranded equivalent before you begin.
Complete the brand licensing fields first, because royalty rate, guarantee and scope decisions shape every later negotiation.
Show every calculation in full, including rates, projections and payment installments, so a partner or advisor can check your numbers.
For portfolio fields, list each patent separately and mark any patent lacking evidence of use as excluded from the package.
Do not contact licensors, brokers, funders or suspected infringers until every field is complete and reviewed against the completion gate.

fields.name: royalty_band_position
fields.prompt: State the royalty rate you will propose or accept for your brand license, then place it inside the operating band practitioners quote, naming the category comparison you used and explaining why your property sits low, middle, or high in that range.
fields.example: Apparel license proposed at 10% of wholesale. Daymond John's working band runs 2% to 15%, with 8% as the normal number and 10% or 12% common [Daymond John — knoob7eUS6Y @ 00:10:34]. Our character is not a hot entertainment property, which would command 12% to 16%, so we sit in the middle rather than the top of the band.

fields.name: minimum_guarantee_math
fields.prompt: Write out the licensee's year-one sales projection, multiply it by the royalty rate to get projected royalties, then set the minimum guarantee and the quarterly payment schedule, showing each calculation step so the numbers can be checked against the half-of-projection rule.
fields.example: Licensee projects $1,000,000 in year-one sales at a 12% royalty, which yields $120,000 projected. Following Stu Seltzer's rule, the guarantee is half of the licensee's own projection [SeltzerLicensingGrp — qx___lyJ5yQ @ 00:04:30], so $60,000, paid as four $15,000 quarterly installments with the first due on contract signing [SeltzerLicensingGrp — MGH55iIT-A0 @ 00:04:03].

fields.name: price_or_volume_lift_test
fields.prompt: Describe how the licensed brand will raise either the selling price or the unit volume of your product compared with an unbranded version, and give the before-and-after numbers, because a royalty paid on the same units at the same price is pure cost.
fields.example: Unbranded jeans retail at $100. With the licensed mark they must clear at least $115, mirroring the jeans test Daymond John applies before taking any license [Daymond John — knoob7eUS6Y @ 00:08:34]. If buyers will not pay the premium or order more units, the royalty simply eats margin on the same pairs, so we walk.

fields.name: licensor_tier_selection
fields.prompt: Name the licensor tier you are targeting, a major studio or a smaller niche property, and explain how its minimum guarantee and paperwork burden fit your brand's current size, cash position, and ability to absorb a guarantee that sales might not cover.
fields.example: We are a small loungewear label, so we will approach niche licensors in their early stages, which often carry very low or zero guarantees [Davie Fogarty — 7U8vYps8fMk @ 00:07:39]. The Oodie's first Warner Brothers drop sold over $500,000 in weeks [Davie Fogarty — 7U8vYps8fMk @ 00:01:35], but we cannot yet carry studio-sized guarantees.

fields.name: licensed_products_definition
fields.prompt: Draft the licensed-products definition clause in plain language, listing every product category included and stating that anything not specifically identified is excluded, so neither party can later argue that a neighboring category falls inside the grant or outside the royalty base.
fields.example: Licensed products are limited to cotton t-shirts, hooded sweatshirts and fleece blankets bearing the approved artwork, and anything not specifically identified is excluded. That wording prevents the scope fight Mayer Brown describes, where parties battled over whether a beer definition included hard seltzers because they were not malt based [Mayer Brown — yRNAVrfCNIE @ 00:58:54].

fields.name: pre_leak_lockdown
fields.prompt: List every domain name, social media handle, and non-disclosure agreement you will secure before any licensing conversation becomes public, with the person responsible and the date each item will be locked, so a leak cannot hold your launch hostage.
fields.example: Before the first licensor call, our operations lead registers the campaign domain plus two spelling variants, claims matching handles on every social platform, and collects signed NDAs from the design agency. Todd Davitz saw a leaked campaign domain bought and the project held hostage on a Friday before a Monday execution [Mayer Brown — yRNAVrfCNIE @ 00:12:33].

fields.name: evidence_of_use_claim_chart
fields.prompt: For each patent you plan to sell or license, identify the company you believe is practicing it, the product involved, and whether a claim chart already maps every claim element to that product, since portfolios without evidence of use do not sell.
fields.example: Patent one maps to a competitor's wireless charging dock; the claim chart covers all independent claim elements and is complete. Patent two has no identified user yet, so it stays out of the package. Clause 8 warns that without a claim chart showing someone practicing the patent, the portfolio will not sell [Clause 8 — t98CwzofUz0 @ 00:34:27].

fields.name: funder_screen_checklist
fields.prompt: Score your portfolio against the litigation funder screen by recording damages potential, likely venue, marking status, prior licenses, and any grant interests, and note which item is weakest, because funders review these before they ever examine technical merit.
fields.example: Damages estimate exceeds $100M across three patent families; venue is favorable; products were marked; one prior license exists; no grant interests apply. Weakest item is the prior license. Funders pass on 19 of every 20 portfolios and check these points before technical merit [IPWatchdog, Inc. — pyi_x9MFGjs @ 00:23:42], so we resolve the license question first.

fields.name: monetization_route_and_split
fields.prompt: Choose your monetization route, a broker-led sale, a funded enforcement campaign, or a direct license, and write down the expected cost share, commission or proceeds split, and the timeline you are budgeting from launch to closing, along with who controls outreach to targets.
fields.example: Broker-led sale chosen. Commission budgeted at 20%, inside the 10-30% range, with closing expected in 6 to 18 months [UpCounsel — xRRc9i7j5A8 @ 00:04:11]. If we instead pursue funded enforcement, the opening split would be 50% owner, 30% funder and 20% law firm [IPWatchdog, Inc. — pyi_x9MFGjs @ 00:07:24]. The broker handles all target contact.

fields.name: outreach_timing_and_infringer_contact
fields.prompt: Set the date your package will be ready, the budget-cycle window you will aim outreach at, and the short list of entities you will contact, and confirm that nobody on your team will approach suspected infringers directly before the package is complete.
fields.example: Package ready March 1; outreach lands before target budgets close, limited to the four entities that matter for our case [International Trade Council — _bueYwQ3iHE @ 00:27:44]. No early contact, since approaching too soon risks silence on a second try [International Trade Council — _bueYwQ3iHE @ 00:46:06], and our broker alone handles suspected infringers.

worksheets.completion_gate: Done when the royalty rate sits inside a quoted band, the minimum guarantee is no more than half of the licensee's year-one royalty projection, the licensed-products definition excludes anything not identified, domains and handles are secured, and every patent offered has a claim chart showing use.

worksheets.title: Permissions, Infringement Response and Royalty Audit Control Sheet
worksheets.purpose: Confirm that every asset in your licensing program is cleared in writing, prepare a disciplined response to infringement on either side, and build the audit rights and statement checks that catch underreported royalties before recovery windows close.
instructions: Pull every contract, license receipt and permission email tied to the assets and products covered by this sheet.
Treat any asset without written permission or a purchased license as uncleared until you can attach proof.
Identify the true seller and clear every independent claim before sending a demand, filing a takedown or launching a redesign.
Compare each royalty statement against the contract line by line, logging flagged lines with the date and the licensee's explanation.
Rule out plain underperformance in writing before you allege underpayment or commission a formal audit.

fields.name: written_permission_inventory
fields.prompt: List every image, music clip, figure, or other third-party asset your licensed product or campaign uses, and beside each one record the written permission or purchased license that covers it, the source, and the scope of use allowed.
fields.example: Hero photo: purchased license, editorial and web use only. Journal figure: cleared through ScienceDirect's get rights and content flow at a zero-fee quote, as Barbara Aboagye demonstrates. Background texture: no watermark, but no license either, so it is removed, because a missing watermark does not mean free [Matthew Anderson — manKMR61ho0 @ 00:10:02].

fields.name: commissioned_work_ownership
fields.prompt: For each commissioned photograph or creative asset, state who holds the copyright under the engagement terms, what uses you as the client are actually allowed, and whether passing the files to a licensee or third party requires a separate written license.
fields.example: Product shoot by a freelance photographer: the photographer keeps copyright, as happens in '90 some percent' of client jobs according to Matthew Anderson [Matthew Anderson — manKMR61ho0 @ 00:02:57]. We may use the images on our site and packaging, but sharing them with our apparel licensee, contests or editorials needs a separate written license from the photographer.

fields.name: registration_timing_plan
fields.prompt: Map your copyright registration schedule for the creative works you license, showing batch sizes, filing cost, expected turnaround, and how each filing lands before client delivery and inside the three-month window after publication to preserve statutory damages and attorney fees.
fields.example: Each month we batch about 1,500 images into one $35 registration with roughly six-week turnaround, using 600-pixel JPEG deposits [B&H Photo Video Pro Audio — 74bQUodJbWY @ 01:16:43]. Registration is filed before files reach the client and within three months of publication [B&H Photo Video Pro Audio — 74bQUodJbWY @ 01:20:24], unlocking $750 to $150,000 per work.

fields.name: true_seller_identification
fields.prompt: Before sending any takedown or demand, record how you identified the true seller behind an unauthorized listing, naming which platform records, corporate searches, domain name lookups, or investigator findings you relied on and what other platforms that seller also uses.
fields.example: The marketplace disclosed the seller's registered business name, which a corporate search tied to a foreign trading company; a domain lookup linked it to two more storefronts. Torys LLP calls the platform the best source for the true seller [Torys LLP — ijF0IyvjXXg @ 00:06:21] and warns that cross-border enforcement can become whack-a-mole [Torys LLP — ijF0IyvjXXg @ 00:02:09].

fields.name: independent_claim_clearance
fields.prompt: For any patent that could read on your licensed product, list every independent claim, including method claims, and explain element by element whether your product contains each one, so you can show the design-around clears the dependent claims as well.
fields.example: The competitor patent has three independent claims: two apparatus and one method. Our redesigned clip omits the spring element in both apparatus claims and skips the heating step in the method claim. Patent Insanity stresses clearing every independent claim [Patent Insanity — Jwz-iMwUtCU @ 00:07:47] and cautions that courts may differ on equivalence [Patent Insanity — Jwz-iMwUtCU @ 00:04:53].

fields.name: infringement_response_protocol
fields.prompt: Write the step-by-step response your team will follow if you receive an infringement claim or discover one, covering who reviews it, how quickly you respond, what you will not do, and how willfulness exposure shapes your settlement position.
fields.example: If an image claim arrives, counsel reviews it within two business days; we neither ignore it nor get defensive, since pulling the image down does not cure the infringement and costs can reach tens of thousands [Matthew Anderson — manKMR61ho0 @ 00:11:29]. On patent claims, willful infringement can bring up to three times damages [LawShelf — WtxlYb996kI @ 00:14:33].

fields.name: audit_clause_terms
fields.prompt: Draft the audit clause terms you will insist on, including the look-back window, the underpayment threshold that shifts audit cost to the licensee, the specific source data the licensee must produce, and a right to review the draft report.
fields.example: Licensee reimburses audit cost when underpayment reaches 5% or more [Authors Guild — NrMiKZwGTD4 @ 00:57:10]. No short look-back cap; a client who accepted two years against an 11-year statute lost most of the window. Source data is named as monthly sales ledgers by SKU, never 'all books and records', and we review any draft report before it goes final.

fields.name: statement_line_check
fields.prompt: Describe how each royalty statement will be checked line by line against the granted territory, the approved product list, and the contracted rate for each sales channel before you accept the report and raise an invoice to the licensee.
fields.example: Our contract sets ten percent for wholesale and twelve for online [Flowhaven — M69XC4rxxQc @ 00:01:48]. Each quarterly report is matched to those rates, the territory list and approved SKUs. Flowhaven's walkthrough flags three lines, an ungranted territory, an unapproved product and a mismatched rate [Flowhaven — HkDV-RELNXc @ 00:03:10], and we invoice only after resolving each flag.

fields.name: red_flag_watchlist
fields.prompt: List the red flags you will monitor across every licensee, such as late statements, unexplained adjustments, spreadsheet-built reports, new statement formats, staff turnover, or mergers, and state which combination of flags will trigger escalation from desktop review to a formal audit.
fields.example: Watchlist: unexplained adjustments, chronically late statements, Excel-made statements, new formats or software, new royalty staff and mergers [Authors Guild — NrMiKZwGTD4 @ 00:08:28]. Two flags in one year move a licensee from desktop review to formal audit, a step worth taking since recoveries reportedly run 5 to 20 times audit cost [Uncover Fraud — 9Fku-QlhyHc @ 00:05:08].

fields.name: underperformance_vs_underpayment
fields.prompt: Before alleging underpayment, explain how you will separate a licensee that is simply selling fewer units from one that is misreporting, naming the sell-through data, trend analysis, or independent sales sources you will compare against the royalty statements received.
fields.example: Royalties fell 30% this half. Before claiming underpayment, we compare reported units with BookScan figures at about $50-65 per ISBN, as Julie Tate does, and run trend analysis to find risky areas [PKF Texas — Z-vXnFsa6zY @ 00:01:29]. Sabarwal Law reminds us a shortfall may simply mean the product is underperforming [Sabarwal Law — 4ZKPBotNzQw @ 00:03:55].

worksheets.completion_gate: Done when every third-party asset has attached written permission, registrations are scheduled before delivery, the audit clause includes a 5% cost-shifting threshold, no short look-back cap, named source data and draft-report review, and each statement has passed a line-by-line check.

worksheets.title: Creative Catalog, Knowledge and Digital Data Licensing Builder
worksheets.purpose: Build a compounding catalog of creative work, knowledge products and digital data that you rent out rather than sell, with delivery specifications, revenue splits, term limits and deletion terms written down before any library, publisher, business client or AI lab signs.
instructions: List every creative work, training product and data set you own, and confirm you hold the rights needed to license each one.
Complete the creative catalog fields before the digital data fields, since delivery standards and splits set your pricing baseline.
Write tags, specifications and clauses in the exact wording you would send to a buyer, not as summary notes.
Record every commission, sync fee share and buyout percentage as a number so routes can be compared side by side.
Do not send files, data exports or signed agreements until the deletion, term limit and exclusivity fields are complete.

fields.name: catalog_compounding_plan
fields.prompt: Set your annual output target for licensable creative works, then show how each new piece multiplies into additional assets such as stems, instrumentals, alternate edits, or cut-downs, and project catalog size and income for years one through five.
fields.example: We write 20 songs a year and turn each into a full mix, instrumental, stems and short edits, building toward 400 licensable assets by year five. Michael Elsner models that climb from roughly $2,000 in year one to $75,000 to $100,000 annually [Elite Music Coaching — D6XhETdysBM @ 00:09:44] while earlier placements keep earning.

fields.name: technical_delivery_spec
fields.prompt: Record the technical delivery specification every licensable track must meet before pitching, including sample rate, bit depth, file format, sample clearance status, available versions, and edit points, and name the person who verifies each file against that specification.
fields.example: Every track ships as a 48 kHz, 24-bit WAV with an instrumental version and stems, and any uncleared sample is stripped before pitching [Majeston — 7t871xx-ysc @ 00:03:23]. Edits land on clean 8- or 16-bar points and end with a sting outro. Our engineer signs off on each export before it enters the catalog folder.

fields.name: supervisor_metadata_tags
fields.prompt: Write the metadata tags for your three strongest tracks the way a music supervisor would search for them, replacing generic words with precise mood, instrument, tempo, and key descriptors, and note where the catalog will be uploaded for discovery.
fields.example: Track one: triumphant, uplifting, victorious; acoustic fingerstyle guitar; not simply happy guitar [Elite Music Coaching — D6XhETdysBM @ 00:06:45]. Track two: clean electric guitar with delay, celebratory. The full catalog with stems, cuts and edits goes to Disco, whose AI tags mood, instruments, tempo and key and helps supervisors discover us [Majeston — 7t871xx-ysc @ 00:02:40].

fields.name: library_route_split
fields.prompt: Compare the routes you are considering for your catalog, such as an agency, a library, or a sub-published library, and write down for each one the share of the sync fee you keep, who holds publishing, and whether exclusivity applies.
fields.example: Agencies take 25-50% of the fee. On a $1,000 placement through a library sub-published by a major, about 25% comes off the top, leaving $375 each for library and composer [Randy McGravey Music — iF_Z6ikfzMo @ 00:11:11]. We reject any library that refuses to share sync fees, as McGravey did with KPM [Randy McGravey Music — iF_Z6ikfzMo @ 00:09:06].

fields.name: advance_and_buyout_terms
fields.prompt: If a publisher offers an advance, record the advance amount, the recoupment term, the buyout percentage you will demand on the unrecouped balance, and confirm that the publisher made the first offer rather than you naming a number first.
fields.example: Publisher sent its offer first, as Producer Royalty advises so we never bid against ourselves [Producer Royalty — gN8CTjqp8lA @ 00:08:20]. Advance of $40,000 under a three-years-or-recoupment term. We require a buyout right at 110 to 125 percent of the unrecouped balance [Producer Royalty — gN8CTjqp8lA @ 00:14:32], so the deal cannot hold us indefinitely.

fields.name: knowledge_term_license
fields.prompt: Describe a course, training, process, or program you could license to a business for deployment across its own clients, stating the one-off sale price, the proposed term license fee, the term length, and what happens to access when the term ends.
fields.example: Our posture-correction course sells for $2,000 to one chiropractor. Licensed to a practice for a fixed period so it can release the material to all of its patients, it is priced at $20,000 [Dr. Lauryn B — QRv3A_DETg4 @ 00:05:53]. The term limit is written in, so we never hand the system over forever [Dr. Lauryn B — QRv3A_DETg4 @ 00:08:11].

fields.name: data_asset_inventory
fields.prompt: Inventory the operational data your company could license to AI labs, such as IT tickets, chat exports, or support records, and note for each set its volume, how it will be anonymized, and the exclusivity position that drives its price.
fields.example: First set: six years of IT tickets, which Jason Varner calls perfect training data because each holds a problem, an action and a fix [Jason Varner — XDzwbT8LWMQ @ 00:05:22]. Second set: anonymized Slack exports. Varner quotes payouts of $100K to $3M plus, driven by exclusivity [Jason Varner — nKuxu_x-s6o @ 00:01:44], so we price exclusive first.

fields.name: deletion_and_model_fate_clause
fields.prompt: Draft the deletion and post-termination clause for your data license, naming every place copies can survive, including labels, caches, backups, and checkpoints, and stating what happens to any model trained on your data once the agreement ends.
fields.example: On termination the licensee deletes source files plus every label, cache, backup and checkpoint derived from them, since clauses limited to source files miss those copies [Archive Trove — y5YpFZxHpYE @ 00:02:01]. Any model trained on our data is retired or retrained without it, because the agreement has to decide the model's fate [Archive Trove — y5YpFZxHpYE @ 00:02:17].

fields.name: dataset_and_cloud_tool_diligence
fields.prompt: Before your data trains a provider's cloud tool or you build on a public dataset, record the license terms you checked, the commercial-use restrictions found, and the audit, regulator, and version-ownership rights you secured in the contract.
fields.example: The public dataset we reviewed uses a custom license barring commercial use, a pattern found in a study where 65% of 221 datasets carried commercial risk [The Linux Foundation — bii4_gwgoBY @ 00:16:50]. For the cloud tool, we secured diligence, regulator and audit access to every model version [Mayer Brown — 5gxaM62YYFk @ 00:25:24] plus ownership of evolutions.

fields.name: exclusivity_and_sales_channel
fields.prompt: State whether each digital asset or dataset will be licensed exclusively at a premium or non-exclusively for volume, where it will be sold, and what commission each marketplace takes compared with selling through a site you own.
fields.example: Our illustration packs sell non-exclusively for volume through a hybrid model: an owned site plus one stock marketplace, because stock sites take 50-80% of each sale [Gait Gain — lvsa9U4qZJA @ 00:10:33]. Custom commissions go out as exclusive licenses at a premium, and every contract states which type applies [Gait Gain — lvsa9U4qZJA @ 00:07:13].

worksheets.completion_gate: Done when every track meets the 48 kHz, 24-bit delivery spec with stems and no uncleared samples, each library route shows the composer's sync share, every advance has a buyout right, knowledge licenses carry term limits, and data licenses name labels, caches, backups, checkpoints and the trained model's fate.
